title: The War in Heaven
setting: Heaven, on the battlefields of the north over three days, as Raphael tells it to Adam in Eden
summary: Abdiel returns to find God’s army already armed, and Michael and Gabriel lead it out. On the first day Abdiel strikes Satan and Michael wounds him; that night Satan invents gunpowder and cannon, which scatter the loyal angels on the second day until they tear up the hills and hurl them. On the third day the Son rides out alone in the chariot of God and drives the rebels over the wall of Heaven, down through Chaos into Hell.

sections.title: Abdiel returns
sections.note: Abdiel flies all night and arrives at dawn to find the loyal army already arrayed. God welcomes him with ‘Servant of God, well done’ for bearing scorn alone for the truth.

sections.title: The armies march
sections.note: God orders Michael and Gabriel to drive the rebels out into Tartarus. The loyal host marches in silent square formation, until the rebel army appears in the north, bristling with spears. Raphael admits how strange it seemed for angel to fight angel.

sections.title: Abdiel faces Satan
sections.note: Satan rides out in a sun-bright chariot. Abdiel, thinking that one who won the argument should win the fight, meets him between the lines; they trade insults about freedom and servitude, and Abdiel tells him: ‘Reign thou in Hell, thy kingdom; let me serve in Heaven’.

sections.title: Abdiel’s stroke; battle joined
sections.note: Abdiel’s blow drives Satan back ten paces to one knee. Michael’s trumpet sounds and the armies crash together in a battle so huge that only God’s limits keep it from wrecking Heaven.

sections.title: Michael duels Satan
sections.note: Satan and Michael exchange threats, then fight like two planets in collision. Michael’s sword, from God’s armoury, cuts Satan’s sword in half and shears into his side: ‘Then Satan first knew pain’. He heals quickly, because angels live in every part and cannot die except by being annihilated.

sections.title: The rest of the first day
sections.note: Gabriel splits Moloch to the waist; Uriel, Raphael and Abdiel overthrow other rebel chiefs. Raphael refuses to name the rebels’ dead heroes. By evening the rebels, feeling fear and pain for the first time, are routed, while the loyal angels stand untired.

sections.title: Night council and a new weapon
sections.note: Satan rallies his chiefs, claiming one day’s survival proves God fallible. Nisroch says pain is the worst of evils and asks for a better weapon. Satan has one ready: substances dug from Heaven’s soil, packed into ‘hollow engines’ and fired.

sections.title: Making the guns
sections.note: The rebels dig up sulphur and saltpetre and cast cannon overnight. Raphael pauses to warn Adam that some of his descendants will reinvent the same thing.

sections.title: Satan’s mock parley
sections.note: At dawn the scout Zophiel warns of the enemy’s approach. Satan, his guns hidden behind his front ranks, pretends to offer peace in a speech full of double meanings.

sections.title: The cannon fire
sections.note: The ranks part, the cannon roar, and the loyal angels are knocked down in heaps, their armour making them clumsy. Satan and Belial crow over them in a string of gunnery puns.

sections.title: The angels hurl the hills
sections.note: The loyal angels throw down their arms, tear up hills by their shaggy tops and bury the cannon and the rebels beneath them. The rebels answer in kind until Heaven is in uproar, and God, who has allowed all of it, turns to his Son.

sections.title: The Father sends the Son
sections.note: After two days of stalemate, God gives the third day to the Son so that the glory of ending the war will be his alone. The Son accepts, promising to take on his Father’s terrors as readily as his mildness.

sections.title: The chariot of Paternal Deity
sections.note: The Son rides out in God’s living chariot, drawn from Ezekiel’s vision: wheels within wheels, four cherubic creatures, eyes everywhere. At his word the uprooted hills return to their places.

sections.title: The rebels harden
sections.note: Seeing his glory only hardens the rebels’ envy. The Son tells the loyal army to stand and watch: since the rebels measure everything by strength, he alone will fight them all.

sections.title: The rout
sections.note: The Son drives over the rebel host with ten thousand thunders, using less than half his strength, and herds them like goats to the crystal wall of Heaven, which opens on the abyss. Rather than face him, they throw themselves over the edge.

sections.title: The fall, the triumph, the warning
sections.note: The rebels fall nine days through roaring Chaos until Hell closes over them, and the Son returns in triumph. Raphael ends by telling Adam why he has told the story: this enemy is now plotting against him, so ‘remember, and fear to transgress’.

glosses.note: Open, level country.
Alternation, as of day and night; ‘grateful’ here means pleasing.
Dutiful, obedient, without the modern sense of fawning.
Readiness; ‘war in procinct’ is war girded up and ready to begin.
Echoes Christ’s parable: ‘Well done, thou good and faithful servant’ (Matthew 25:21); ‘the better fight’ recalls ‘fight the good fight’ (1 Timothy 6:12).
In Greek myth the deepest pit of the underworld, where the defeated Titans were imprisoned.
A square military formation.
Standing in the way (Latin obvius); no hill or valley breaks their ranks.
Warlike, arrayed for battle.
Supposed, expected.
Foolish.
An assembly or council; Satan grandly calls his rebels ‘Gods’ in council.
An answer, in story order, to Satan’s own boast in Book I: ‘Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven’.
A Hebrew cry of praise, originally ‘save, we pray’.
A vault or canopy, here made of flying fire.
Astrological language: planets in a hostile position, ‘opposition’ meaning directly across the sky from each other.
Piercing, cutting through. A ‘discontinuous wound’ is a medical term for a gash that breaks the body’s continuity.
Kidneys.
Asmodeus, the demon of the Book of Tobit whom Raphael drove away; fittingly, Raphael defeats him here. Adramelech was an idol of the Assyrians (2 Kings 17:31).
An Assyrian god, in whose temple King Sennacherib was murdered (2 Kings 19:37).
Sulphur and saltpetre (nitre), which with charcoal make gunpowder.
A kindling match or fuse for firing the guns.
Satan’s speech is full of gunnery puns: ‘overture’ (an opening), ‘discharge’, ‘touch’, ‘propound’.
Explode, fire off; a ‘tire’ is a volley or row of guns.
Belial keeps up the joke: heavy cannonballs as weighty ‘terms’, which knock the enemy off their feet so they cannot ‘understand’ (stand under) them or walk ‘upright’.
Hurling, throwing.
One who sits beside a ruler and shares his authority.
From Ezekiel’s visions (chapters 1 and 10): wheels within wheels full of eyes, four living creatures with four faces, a crystal firmament and a sapphire throne.
Gems worn on the breastplate of Israel’s high priest (Exodus 28:30).
Echoes Hesiod’s Theogony, where an anvil dropped from heaven would fall nine days before reaching the earth; Book I has the rebels lying nine days on the burning lake.

famous.why: God’s welcome to Abdiel, praising the one who stood alone and bore universal reproach, ‘far worse to bear than violence’.
Abdiel redefines servitude: to serve the worthy is freedom, while Satan is ‘to thyself enthralled’.
Michael’s sword shears Satan’s side: ‘Then Satan first knew pain’, and he bleeds the strange nectar of angels.
The chariot of Paternal Deity, Milton’s blazing rebuild of Ezekiel’s vision, is the most spectacular image in the poem.
The rebels throw themselves headlong from Heaven, and ‘Nine days they fell’: the moment Book I picks up from.

themes: Force against reason: Abdiel wins the argument first, and only then the fight.
War between immortals is a stalemate, and Milton makes much of it comic, with puns, cannon and hurled mountains.
Freedom and servitude are redefined: serving God is liberty, serving one’s own pride is slavery.
The Son wins not by violence alone but by God’s gift of glory, and uses less than half his strength.
art: The Son in the living chariot of God, its wheels full of eyes and flame, driving the rebel angels like a herd over the crystal wall of Heaven into the dark abyss.
